paragraphs.text: the four levels of creation are traditionally categorized as domem (inanimate), tzomeach (vegetative), chai (animal), and medaber (human with speech) The term 'memallel' is sometimes used as a designation for the human level with speech capacity, emphasizing the faculty or potential to emit words or utterances.
humans can convey complex abstract ideas through language

The suggestion that 'memallel' refers to one who utters words, regardless of whether those words are consciously heard or accepted, while 'medaber' implies speech that is actually heard or accepted, is a hypothesis without clear classical source support There is no explicit authoritative text differentiating these according to experiential reception or acceptance of speech.

question_html:
Memallel vs. M'daber vs. M'Siach

Related to this question and the comments on it, because originally by mistake I called the speaking kingdom Medaber instead of Memallel.

Are porpoises considered Memallel or Chai?

Why is Memallel chosen to be the label for the fourth kingdom? I take it part of it is that speech that is not heard or accepted as per below, is not called Dibbur, so I can see what Medaber is. Sicha is casual conversation. Mila refers to words.

https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Translation:Likutei_Etzot#DIBBUR_-_Speech

Speech (Dibbur) that doesn't get heard or accepted can't be called "speech" at all. Tikkun haDibbur, when it's heard and accepted, comes by saying words of praise of the True Tzaddikim. This is Tikkun haKlali, General Remedy, for your speech (29:1,2).
But what is Memallel versus now there's Dinbur and Mila so two things to differentiate from, and the answer coming to me, that Memallel is one who utters words. Medaber is someone whose speech (or written words?) is heard or accepted. M'Siach is someone who converses, that you can chat with. Is this correct, or no?

Also, Dibbur can refer to written speech, so one could be illiterate yet still speaks the words of the language and is therefore Memallel. I guess M'daber is therefore more inclusive, because it includes also up someone who writes but doesn't speak. Since speech came and comes before writing, I guess I've answered my own question. Unless I'm mistaken

anchor_terms: דומם, צומח, חי, מדבר (Inanimate, Vegetative, Animal, Speaking)
research_plan.context: The fourth kingdom here means the fourth LEVEL OF CREATION (inanimate, vegetative, animal, human speaking), NOT Daniel, Rome, Persia or prophetic empires. M'Siach is the questioner's transliteration of conversation (שיחה), NOT משיח/Messiah. The proposed heard/accepted versus mere utterance distinction is a HYPOTHESIS TO CHECK, never a fact to repeat. A quotation in the question is not independently verified evidence. Do not generalize a spiritual statement into a lexical definition. Separate ordinary definitions from a specific author's usage.
references: בראשית א:יח (Genesis 1:18) – creation of living creatures and distinction of levels
מדרש רבה בראשית פ״ח (Bereishit Rabbah 8) – exegesis on creation and speech
הגדה של פסח, סעיף 'ארבעה בנים' (Haggadah, Four Sons) – classical differentiation of levels
רמב״ם, לשון הרמב״ם הלכות תלמוד תורה פרק ב (Rambam, Hilchot Talmud Torah 2) – on language and speech faculties
זוהר בראשית, פרשה ו (Zohar Bereshit 6) – mystical explanations of speech and creation

sources.text: Many of the laws and details regarding the creation of tefillin are oral traditions that trace back to Moses, known as halachah leMoshe miSinai.1 Received from G‑d atop Mount Sinai, they were passed down by Moses to Joshua, and from there down to the leaders and sages of each generation. These specifications are not hinted at in Scripture, nor can they be deduced logically. Yet they are far from arbitrary. As Maimonides writes, it is appropriate to contemplate these decrees and provide an explanation for them whenever possible. With this in mind, here are just a few explanations that the mystics give as to why tefillin needs to be made of animal hide. Harnessing Impulses When we put on tefillin, we place one box upon the left arm (signifying action) opposite the heart (the seat of the emotions) and the other upon the head (the seat of the intellect). When doing so, we have in mind the submission of one's mind, heart and actions to the Almighty. On the one hand, we do not simply follow the impulses of the heart (since we can easily be tempted), but on the other hand, we can’t simply follow our intellect (as that path can be harsh and cold). Based on this, some explain that by placing sacred leather parchments in a box made of animal hide, we subdue and transform our animalistic desires and impulses and use them in our service of G‑d. Elevating All of Creation The mystics explain that the world can be separated into four major components: domem (inanimate/mineral), tzomeach (vegetation), chai (animal) and medaber (humankind). In the process of preparing the hides and making the tefillin, certain herbs (tzomeach) and water (domem) are used to process the hides (chai). When the person (medaber) performs the mitzvah of tefillin, he is gathering and elevating all four components of creation and demonstrating how G‑d is the master and creator of all.2 See Menachot 35a. See talk by the Lubavitcher Rebbe, 19th of Kislev 5743, Torat Menachem 5743, vol. 2, p. 661; see also Rama, Torat Ha'olah.
sources.title: Why Are Tefillin From Animal Hide?

sources.question_context: What is the source for the idea that all matter is either domem (lifeless), tzomeach (plant), chai (animal), or medaber (speaker)? I sometimes find this quoted places (in articles and divrei Torah), but have not been able to find a source? Is it a Gemara? A Midrash? A Chasidic teaching? I even found this, where the Vilna Gaon says "it is known": http://dafyomireview.com/article.php?docid=270&style=print
sources.relevance_reason: Traces the classical source of the four categories domem, tzomeach, chai, and medaber in Jewish thought, citing multiple medieval Jewish commentators and explaining the concept as a category of creation.
sources.text: The actual source is from non-Jewish naturalists, dating in some form or another back to Aristotle , who also believed in some sense that man is in a different category ( teleologically, and therefore categorically ). It was later refined into a rigorous taxonomic system . The idea was picked up by Jewish scholars from the Medieval Era, though some of them use the word מרגיש instead of חי to refer to animal life. This includes the Kuzari (1:31-39), by the Radak (in his comments to Yirmiyahu 10:8), Rabeinu Bachaye (to Shemos 34:35 and Kad HaKemach, Pesach 1), R. Yehoshua ibn Shueib (Parshas Emor), R. Yosef Albo (Sefer HaIkkarim 2:30), Abarbanel (Parshas Pinchas ch. 28), and is hinted to in the Meiri to Avodah Zara 42b. After this period, it becomes extremely widespread in Jewish thought, appearing almost a dozen times in the writings of the Shelah, for example
sources.title: Source for Categorization of Matter

Is it, in meaning, associated with the 4-letter name which is replaced by it, or is it a distinct name with separate attributes?

Answer 2 (Rabbi Kaii): Sorry, I don't know how to answer this without "essay" format. It's a very good question, but to properly answer it, there is a lot to get through. I have done my best to not condense it too much, and I welcome questions, and suggest reading up the citations for further study. The Name of Adnut, Lordship, should be taken to mean that Hashem is the absolute Master of nature. He created it and is creating it every moment, from absolute and utter nothingness, and is therefore in complete control. This is true Lordship (see many places, e.g. Sefer Maamarim 5659 Sukkot Night 2 ). This is why it is sometimes also associated with the aspect of " din " (it contains those letters in it - see R' Yosef Chayyim's Aderet Eliyahu on Parashat Shoftim ; See also the Baalei Berit Avram on Parashat Shoftim ), because "natural law" appears to be "logical". "Survival of the fittest", "one must earn one's bread with the sweat of one's brow" etc. Justice is cold, harsh, but fair - but certainly not "compassionate". If you combine the Name with "E-l", you get the same gematria as "tzav", which the Arizal associates with idolatry. In this world, we can look around, and say "where's the compassion?" and make a mistake and think that there's no Hashem, and this is the essence of idolatry (see Derech Mitzvotecha Mitzvat Korban Pesach ). However, there is a famous combination of the Names Adnut and Havaya, which is taken to mean that we restore this seeming schism when we look closely and see that everything actually is Hashem's compassion - Havaya is all there is. Shem Adnut also has the same gematria as "Heichal", i.e. the Beit Hamikdash, the seat of Hashem's righteous judges, who issue righteous judgements, and this creates this very combination of the Names, in a "higher unification" ( Chomat Anach on Shoftim 2:18 - see what I wrote here for more). Interestingly, the Beit Hamikdash is the one place where we pronounce Hashem's Name, instead of pronouncing it b'Shem Adnut! By studying Hashem's Laws (i.e. His righteousness and justice), we see the compassion. It's only right that if I have more money than I need, and someone else has less than they need, that I should give him some of my money. It's fair (tzeddaka = tzedek), but it's also a clear demonstration of how when we follow Hashem's laws, we are producing compassion*. Another example are the laws of slavery, i.e. treat your slave like a mentsch. It's only fair, but it shows the deep compassion we should have for every human being. See Hemshech Samech Vav , especially the later ma'amarim for extensive coverage on this concept of how halacha reveals Hashem. See also Likkutei Torah of the Alter Rebbe on Parashat Bechukotai . If you want to get specific, and go deeper (as your question and comments indicate), this Name is the name of Malchut of Atzilut. Much of what we said above is very similar to other vertlach about Elokim. I.e. when we see through the "mask" of the world, that all is Him, we are "shown to know, that Hashem is Elokim... Ein Old Milvado" (Devarim 4:39). So what's the similarity with Elokim and Adnut? Well, they both pertain to the obscuring, the "tzimtzum" Hashem creates in order for there to be this world. Elokim is His Name of Gevura, which represents His power of restriction and limitation. He uses it in order to restrict His Light so that the world, paradoxically, can be revealed . A nice mashal used is that of the sun. If the earth were inside the sun, we would not be able to see it, as it would be totally outshined by the sun's light. Therefore, the earth is at a distance from the sun, and only lit up by "rays" that have left the sun and travelled a long way, and now we can see the earth (see Derech Mitzvotecha Haamanut Elokut 6). This is another way of saying that if we saw just how good and compassionate Hashem is, we would lose our free will in that we would choose Him without a second thought, but because He "hides behind cold, harsh nature", we have an opportunity to choose Him from our own free will. So, Elokim is like a "shield" to Havaya (see Tanya Shaar Hayichud VehaEmuna ), restricting our perception so we are not blinded and nullified by Hashem. This is where Shem Adnut comes in. Hashem's Malchut is His power of Speech - He speaks the world into creation. In order for there to be a world that is, so to speak, "separate" from Him, He needs to use His power of Gevura - as above - and condense His Light and Being into letters, speaking words, as it is written in Sefer Maamarim 5659 Sukkot Night 2: וז״ש כבוד מלכותך כו׳ וגבורתך ידברו, דבכדי שיהיו האותיות דמלכות בבחי׳ יש, שיוכל להיות מקור להוות עולמות בי״ע, זהו ע״י וגבורתך דוקא, בחי׳ גבורה דז״א, לצמצם את האור, ועי״ז דוקא נעשו האותיות בבחי׳ יש כו׳ And this is the meaning of what is written: "The glory of Your kingship... and Your might they will speak." For in order that the letters of Malchut should be in the category of "somethingness", such that they can be the source for the coming into being of the worlds of Creation (BiYA), this is specifically through "Your Might," the aspect of Gevura of Ze'ir Anpin, to contract the light. And specifically through this the letters become in the category of "somethingness", etc. Why? Well, words are very superficial and external in comparison to the concepts they are representing - like a mashal. They are "just" words, and therefore this is a great contraction and restriction of Hashem's Light. It is through these words that He creates the world we live in, i.e. the world of nature that I spoke about above. The fact that He is speaking the world into creation is indeed why He is the absolute and utter Master and Lord of the world (it's His story!), hence the Name Adnut. For a bit more detail - the power of Malchut is the most external power of Hashem's Being. The world of Atzilut is not a "mashal", it is genuinely His very Being, although it has being somewhat restricted and limited by Gevura. What this means is that He identifies with Atzilut, He speaks in the first person. "My Chochma", "My Gevura", "My Malchut". Still, the worlds created by His Malchut are from Him, but He considers them "external" to Him - we are separate from Him. Therefore there is a transition point and this happens in Malchut of Atzilut, part of which actually becomes the highest point of the created worlds. This is Shem Adnut, and is also referred to as the Shechina, the Kise HaKavod, Mimaaleh Kol Almin, and the parsa / parochet . It is where Hashem "puts on His mask" as it were ( hester panim ; see Worldmask by R' Tatz ), and hides behind nature. We must know though that nature is a perfect mashal of Him (i.e. the words He speaks to create the mashal are all about Him, the Nimshal, authentically), and therefore if we study it through the lens of Torah, and particularly, study His Laws (as we we wrote above), we will see through the mashal, and create gilui panim ; this Yichud Elyon cited by Chomat Anach above. tl;dr: Havaya - Hashem's Name that is utterly beyond. Pertains to "being", but also pertains to His lofty goodness and compassion. Elokim - Hashem's power of Gevura - restriction and limitation. Adnut - Hashem's Name that is associated with His power of action and creation (Malchut), where, after He limits Himself by hiding behind nature, His Kingship is revealed as His being utterly in charge of nature - Lording over it. Our job is to realise that Hashem's goodness is still here in the world of nature, and is only hidden in order to allow free will. We study His Torah, and realise that the Master of Nature is actually one and the same as Havaya, the Infinite, Transcendent Havaya, Who is Good and Compassionate. Nature only exists due to His immense power of Gevura that gives us this impression, but in truth, He is Elokim, and the Master of Nature - all is One. For a thoroughly clear, comprehensive treatment of this topic, please see this Torat Chaim by the Mittler Rebbe, of blessed and righteous memory: בעז״ה תורת אדמו״ר הרב ר׳ דובער פרשה וארא באברוסק שנת תקפ״ד יום א - הוא אהרן ומשה . You'll find he doesn't mention din at all, and focuses primarily on Hashem's Kingship and the concept of the unification with Havaya, through Pesukei Dezimra and the first two verses of Shema. * There's an amazing Chida (Rosh David, Vayachel, quoting Parashat Derachim) that explains how this fulfils Hashem's "first thought" to create the world with din , instead of "combining" it with mercy. We actually transform the din into mercy, so the world is no longer a "combination", but actually made out of din , like He always wanted!

Answer 3 (Mr E.): B"H In Tanya, Shaar Hayichud vihaemunah chapter 7 , the Alter Rebbe contrasts the names Adnus and Havayah, saying that the former is how Hashem is manifested within the division of space and time (malchis, kingship), while Havayah refers to how He creates all past, present and future as one essential point: Chapter 7 פרק ז The Alter Rebbe explained in the previous chapters that the Scriptural statement that “in the heavens above and upon the earth below, there is none other” is not intended to negate the existence of another god. Rather, it tells us that Divine Unity is such that there is no true existence other than G‑d, for all created beings are completely nullified in relation to Him and are united with Him. This is not perceived by them nor manifest in them only because of the tzimtzum which conceals the Divine life-force that continuously brings about their existence ex nihilo. Being unable to perceive this life-force, they consider themselves to be independently existing entities. This concealment, of course, applies only to created beings but not to their Creator. From the Divine perspective, there is no concealment whatsoever, inasmuch as Havayah and Elokim are truly one: the concealment effected by Elokim thus does not act as a concealment for Havayah. The Alter Rebbe will now explain how the above enables us to understand the teaching of the Zohar that Shema Yisrael is “higher-level Unity” and Baruch shem is “lower-level Unity.” Were Divine Unity merely to signify the existence of one G‑d, it would be impossible to speak of higher and lower levels of Unity. According to the above explanation, however, that Divine Unity means the nullity of created beings and their unity with G‑d, it is indeed possible to speak of two diverse levels of Unity. In this sense, “higher-level Unity” refers to the Divine faculty of creative speech (otherwise known as malchut), considered at the stage in which it is still found within its source. By way of analogy, the seminal letters of a person’s speech are first encapsulated within his thought and emotions, which will ultimately be responsible for his subsequent speech. (The Rebbe notes that “this was explained in Part I, chs. 20-21.”) The same is true Above: When supernal creative speech is at the stage in which it is still included within the supernal attributes—which, being infinite, are too lofty to serve as a source of creation, for it is inherently limited to space and time—creation as it exists in its source is united with G‑d at the higher level of Unity. Its manner of nullification is then similar to the nullification of the sun’s rays as they are found within the sun-globe. When, however, the Divine creative power of speech (or malchut), after undergoing a process of tzimtzumim, descends to a level at which it is able to serve as a source for creation, then the term “lower-level Unity” applies. Created beings at this level cannot be said to be completely and utterly nullified. For inasmuch as this level becomes the actual source of created beings, they must perforce have some measure of identity in relation to it. Although this level, too, is pervaded by the Ein Sof-light which unites with the Divine faculty of creative speech, this unification is nevertheless one of “lower-level Unity,” wherein created beings are seen to have some measure of existence—albeit a nullified form of existence, but existence nonetheless. With the above in mind, we may now understand the statement in the holy Zohar that the verse Shema Yisrael is yichuda ilaah (“higher-level Unity”) and that the verse Baruch shem kvod malchuto leolam vaed is yichuda tataah (“lower-level Unity”). וּבָזֶה יוּבַן מַה שֶּׁכָּתוּב בַּזֹּהַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ, דְּפָסוּק "שְׁמַע יִשְׂרָאֵל" – הוּא "יִחוּדָא עִילָּאָה", וּ"בָרוּךְ שֵׁם כְּבוֹד מַלְכוּתוֹ לְעוֹלָם וָעֶד" – הוּא "יִחוּדָא תַּתָּאָה", The connection between the last mentioned verse and Divine Unity is now explained: For1 vaed is equivalent to echad through the substitution of letters.2 כִּי "וָעֶד" הוּא "אֶחָד" בְּחִלּוּפֵי אַתְוָון. The alef of echad interchanges with the vav of vaed since both letters belong to the same group of letters, viz., alef, hey, vav, yud (which, the Rebbe notes, are known as otiyot hahemshech, the “connective letters”). sources.question_context: The soul has 5 names , and one of them is Chaya. Chaya is also a word for " animal " (a wild animal, halachically ) . I want to know, is there anything animal-like (or "wild"), about the Chaya that is brought down in the sources? Is there any reason for the usage of the same name or is it just lexical overlap (they are both חי " alive ") This Heichalot Rabbati is interesting. I've seen the term Chaya there translated as "animal" or "creature" before. By the way, I ask this with the utmost respect. I am not trying to imply that this soul level is truly "animalistic", lowly, or any other negative connotation. If there is a connection, it will be about something comparable between them that is a loftiness of some sort, I imagine.
sources.relevance_reason: Offers explanation and context on the term Chaya, related to the animal soul and its place between vegetative and human levels, which adds useful context to the terminology around kingdoms of creation including Memallel and Chai.
sources.text:
Answer 1 (Rabbi Kaii): Here is a relationship (Sha'arei Kedusha 3:2): אחר נברא החי והם בהמות ועופות וכו'. ובהם גוף ונפש דומם ונפש צומחת ונוסף עליו נפש החיה הנקרא נפש הבהמית והתנועה וההרגש : Afterwards, the animate beings (Chay) were created, referring to animals and birds etc. They have the body (Guf) and soul (Nefesh) of the inanimate (Domem), as well as the soul (Nefesh) of the vegetative (Tzome’ach), and in addition, they also have the soul (Nefesh) of the animate (Chayah), which is called the animalistic soul (Nefesh HaBehamit) and includes the power of movement and the sensatory powers. [borrowed Amiram Markel's translation]

Answer 2 (Nissim Nanach): There is a grand Chaya in heaven as we know from the Baraita of R' Akiba One Chaya stands in RKYA and its name is Yisrael and inscribed on its forehead is " Yisrael ." It stands in the middle of the RKIA and says: Barekhu et-H' the Blessed. And all the Supernal Allies reply: Blessed is H' forever and ever. אמר רבי עקיבא: חיה אחת עומדת ברקיע, ושמה ישראל, וחקוק על מצחה ישראל, עומדת באמצע הרקיע ואומרת: ברכו את ה' המבורך; וכל גדודי מעלה עונים ואומרים: ברוך ברוך ה' המבורך לעולם ועד. To me I envision an entity that's the "party animal" who as we see here is engaged in pep and praise; so it's a level to aspire to and which one can easily attain. Also I think Jung's "anima" and "animus" was inspired by Chaya. anima /ăn′ə-mə/ noun The inner self of an individual; the soul. In Jungian psychology. The unconscious or true inner self of an individual, as opposed to the persona, or outer aspect of the personality. The American Heritage® Dictionary of the English Language, 5th Edition • More at Wordnik Being opposite to the embodied sexual identity, Anima and Animus are most easily related to the erotic encounters and partners and inspire the creative and artistic imagination. https://iaap.org/jung-analytical-psychology/short-articles-on-analytical-psychology/anima-and-animus-2/ This aspect of the animus seems to relate to the Chaya's fervor in prayer, and seems to be reflected in Likutei Moharan 2 which discusses how prayer and the Berit are interdependent. And Tikkun hamedameh and dreams .. even animals dream

sources.question_context: If animals don't have spirits ( Does anyone have a proof text that animals *don't* have spirits? ), then what is the meaning of nishmat ruach chayim in Bereshit 7:22? And in what way does it differ from the nishmat chayim of humans? See Derekh HaShem here paragraph beginning with "והנה". A partial quotation: כי אין נפש הבעלי חיים אלא דבר גשמי, מן הדקים שבגשמיות ― Although animals may have a soul, it is not a spiritual entity, it is the most fine of physical entities. If so what is meant by 'the most fine physical entity'? And if only the human soul is spiritual, what does it mean? Cause aren't both humans and animal soul non-physical (non-touchable, not visible etc.)
sources.relevance_reason: Discusses the nature of the animal soul and human soul, including references to domem, tzomeach, chai, and medaber, the four levels of creation, offering insight into classifications of soul and speech.
sources.text:
Answer 1 (ray): in chovos halevavos shaar bechina "It is proper that you should know that the whole world (even inanimate things - Tov Halevanon) is synthesized of the physical and the spiritual, so intimately mixed and fused, that each of them sustains the other, like body and soul in living creatures." pas lechem commentary there on the words "like body and soul (nefesh) in living creatures": the soul prolongs and sustains the body. When the soul leaves the body, the body immediately inanimates and decomposes. Likewise, the body sustains the animal soul in animals, and when the animal soul leaves the animal's body, it (the animal soul) ceases and nullifies. Likewise, for the nefesh tzomachat (plant soul) in plants. For the nefesh medaberet (human soul) we can say the same regarding its existing in this physical world, because immediately after the human soul leaves the body, it returns to its place in the higher worlds [as written (Eccl. 12:7) "Then shall the dust return to the earth as it was: and the spirit shall return unto G-d who gave it."]. hence the animal soul is lower level than human soul and cannot exist independently of the animal body unlike human higher soul which is independent of the human body and can continue to exist without it.

Answer 2 (Jerusalem Programmer): בע"ה Clearly by means of logic and reason, not every Rabbi/Sage of ancient past can be correct since there are so many disagreements and both diverging and conflicting opinions can be found in all matters. So by means of logic and reason: not every Rabbi is correct. That being said, if I am not mistaken, according to Kabbalah there are only two things that exist: 1.) the Creator, and 2.) the Creation which includes the universe and everything that it contains including all physical Creation(s) and all spiritual Creation(s) which preceded the physical Creation(s). Since we are all One Being (i.e. the Creation), we are all one interconnected Being. According to Torah, everything that has life has Nishmat Ruach Chayim, i.e. the Breath of the Spirit/Wind of Life. And Who is the Source of Life, if not the Creator, HaKadosh (Baruch Hu), the Holy One (Blessed Be He)? We all have the Breath of Spirit of Life within us, and this includes every creature that exists that breathes. So if this one Rabbi Derech HaShem says that animals do not have souls, I would challenge him that he contradicts something that is written in the Written Torah that says otherwise. And it is likely that another Rabbi could be found in ancient history who would disagree with Derech HaShem's opinion. Shabbat Shalom.

Answer 3 (Loewian): The "animal soul" is entirely subjective and atheistic. It exists entirely in a physical, instinctual, hedonic, and sensory world. While (at least in higher life forms) there may be a fair level of social cognition and even altruistic behavior and empathy, there is no possibility of ever attaining human levels of consciousness of truth and morality. Arguably, this is represented by the unique human level of language, whereby which all of reality, including theology, can be labeled and conceptualized. This isn't to say that the distinctly human aspects of cognition have no roots in more primitive animal roots, or that there aren't many humans who don't really elevate themselves actually above the basic animalistic instincts. Nonetheless, actual animals don't even have the potential for the distinct moral and rational worldview and behavior that makes humans the ultimate goal of creation. See also e.g.: http://www.daat.ac.il/encyclopedia/value.asp?id1=3624 *see e.g. Targum Onkelos on "נפש חיה" which he translates "רוח ממללא".

sources.question_context: Midbar is commonly translated as desert or wilderness. It seems to come from the root davar (word) so I'm guessing the idea is that a midbar is a place where survival is most evidently dependent on the word of Hashem. Is this right? I've found sources on line that say that the Sahara is the third biggest desert in the world with the Arctic as the second biggest and Antarctica as the biggest. I have no doubt that the Sahara qualifies as a midbar. My question is does the Arctic and Antarctica qualify as a midbar in loshon kodesh? They certainly seem to be places where survival is not easy.
sources.relevance_reason: Explains the linguistic root and conceptual connection between midbar (wilderness) and medaber (speaking), relevant to clarifying the term Memallel versus M'daber and their links to speech and environment.
sources.text:
Answer 1 (Yaacov Deane): The noun Midbar is best translated as wilderness , not necessarily desert . The distinction being that a wilderness is a place devoid of human habitation and settlements. The term desert , although coincidentally usually not conducive to human settlement, is only about a lack of precipitation, rainfall or snowfall. And to emphasize, it doesn’t necessarily imply a lack of availability of water. A desert can be filled with wellsprings, underground aquifers or like the continent of Antarctica can be covered with ice and snow because whatever precipitation has ever fallen there over the millennia has not evaporated because of the extreme and continuous cold. So returning to the subject of wilderness being devoid of human settlement, the Torah, in its categorization of different types of creations, has four general categories of: inanimate objects דומם (things which are silent and do not have their own power of locomotion), plants צומח (things which sprout, usually, but not limited to sprouting from the ground), animals חיות (meaning things which do not sprout and which possess the power of self-locomotion. They may also be able to make noises and even possess some form of communication other than speech.) and humanoids מדבר (beings which have the power of speech, either oral or written or both). And this underlines the association of wilderness מדבר (pronounced Midbar) and humanoid מדבר (pronounced M’Daber, meaning speak or speech) settlement. That a wilderness can be profusely filled with all kinds of life, but is devoid of speech.

Answer 2 (Shmuel): Rabbi Yonathan Sacks z"l explained once that the meaning behind the word "midbar" is to mean (COVENANT & CONVERSATION The Wilderness and the Word, Bamidbar 5768) : The Hebrew word midbar, wilderness, has the same root as the word dabar/davar, meaning “word” or “thing.” It has the same letters as medabber, “speaking.” It is in the wilderness that the Israelites hear revelation, the word or speaking of G-d There's a famous Midrash (see for example here ) that explains why the Torah has been given in the midbar. Why was the Torah not given in the Holy Land, Eretz Yisrael? The answer lies, tells the Midrash, in the fact that a midbar has no ownership on itself. A midbar belongs to no one. So too, everyone has an equal claim to the Torah (see also Midrash Tanchuma, Chukas 21:1) Elsewhere , Rabbi Sacks explains the deeper meaning behind the reason why the Torah was given in the midbar: The giving of the Torah in the wilderness is an essential feature of Jewish history. Had the Israelites received the Torah in the land, it would be indissolubly associated with the land. Exile would mean the end of the covenant. It would make no more sense to keep Torah while in exile than to obey the laws of Russia while living in Spain. What made the G-d of Israel different was the fact that He was sovereign of the universe, not a local deity. That is why the Jewish people survived dispersion. Only the G-d of everywhere can be found and worshipped anywhere. I would strongly recommend this article, to further grasp the essence of the word "midbar" and the relationship between the giving of the Torah and us being in exile. https://www.rabbisacks.org/covenant-conversation/bamidbar/wilderness-and-revelation/
sources.title: What does midbar mean?

sources.question_context: I'm looking for Rabbinical/Kabbalical explanations for the resemblance between animals and humans, especially mammals and apes. This is [partially only] influenced by the series of question on the 613 body parts vs 613 Mitzvos. Does this likeness relate to the similarity in souls, obligations etc vs humans and Jews?
sources.relevance_reason: Provides rabbinic insights on species boundaries and intermediates between inanimate, vegetative, animal, and human, giving background relevant to classification but less directly focused on Memallel/M’daber distinctions.
sources.text:
Answer 1 (Joel K): R. Chaim Vital, Etz Chaim 42:1 : מ"ש חכמי הטבע כי בין הדומם והצומח הוא הקורא"לי הנקרא אלמוגים ובין הצומח והחי הוא אדני השדה הנזכר במסכת כלאים שהוא כמין כלב גדל בקרקע וטבורו נשרש בקרקע ויונק משם וכשחותכין הטבור שלו מת ובין החי והמדבר הוא הקוף .‏ [T]hat which the scientists wrote that intermediate between inanimate matter and plants there is coral, and between plants and animal life there is the adnei hasadeh (mentioned in Masechet Kilayim) which is a kind of dog that grows from the ground and which is umbilically connected to the ground from which it is sustained and if one cuts that cord it dies, and intermediate between animals and humans is the monkey . So, if apes are viewed as an intermediate category between animals and humans, it makes sense that they would resemble the human form in certain ways.

Answer 2 (Joel K): If you’re looking for practical ramifications of the resemblance between humans and apes, then consider R. Yose’s opinion in Kilayim 8:5 : וְאַדְנֵי הַשָּׂדֶה, חַיָּה. רַבִּי יוֹסֵי אוֹמֵר, מְטַמְּאוֹת בָּאֹהֶל כָּאָדָם.‏ The adnei hasadeh is a wild animal. R. Yose says, it[s carcass] imparts impurity in a tent, like a human. What is this adnei hasadeh creature? Tiferet Yisrael ad loc. : בר נש דטור. נ"ל דר"ל וואלדמענש הנקרא אוראנגאוטאנג והוא מין קוף גדול בקומת וצורת אדם ממש. רק שזרעותיו ארוכים ומגיעין עד ברכיו ... מיהו ת"ק ס"ל דאע"ג דדומה לאדם בפרצופו ואבריו. אפ"ה כשמת דינו רק כשאר נבילות. ואמ"ט באהל.‏ This refers to the “mountain man”. It appears to me that it means the “wildman” which is called orangutan. This is a type of large ape, of the actual size and appearance of a human, except that it has long arms which reach to its knees ... However, the Tanna Kamma holds that although it is similar to a human in its face and limbs, nevertheless, when it dies it is subject to the same rules as other animal carcasses, and does not impart impurity in a tent. So, according to Tiferet Yisrael, R. Yose holds that carcasses of orangutans (and maybe other great apes as well?) have some of the same laws of impurity as human corpses (and which do not apply to other animals) owing to their physiological similarities. The other sages, in contrast, believe that orangutans' similar appearance to humans is not sufficient cause for their carcasses to impart impurity in the same way as humans corpses do.

Answer 3 (David the Prince): To give you my own opinion, a similar resemblance between mankind and animals is what we would expect if there was one Creator God. This can be related to how a painter has his own style of painting and that style is reflected across his creations. Similarly, with one Almighty Creator God we should expect to (and we do) find similar characteristics not only shared within the animal kingdom but across all of creation mind you with each aspect of creation having their variously assigned functions and purposes.
sources.title: Rabbinical explanation of the physiological resemblance between animals and humans
